analysis.investment_thesis: Jupiter Life Line Hospitals has a decent business with 18% ROCE and strong revenue growth, but the Magic Formula rejects it on valuation — at 3.5% earnings yield (EBIT INR 297 Cr / EV ~INR 8,430 Cr), it trades at nearly 3x the 12% threshold I require. You're paying a premium growth multiple for a capital-intensive hospital business that generated negative FCF of -INR 67 Cr in FY25.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 22% CAGR (5Y) with EBITDA margins expanding from 24% to 25%, showing operating leverage
Finance costs collapsed from INR 44 Cr (FY22) to INR 11 Cr (FY25), indicating disciplined capital structure before recent expansion debt
OCF positive all 5 years; FY25 OCF of INR 253 Cr is strong, suggesting the core hospital business generates real cash
key_risks: Earnings Yield of ~3.5% (EBIT/EV) is far below my 12% minimum — the stock is priced for perfection at 26.6x EV/EBITDA
Massive capex cycle underway: INR 321 Cr capex in FY25 + CWIP of INR 296 Cr; took on INR 403 Cr new debt after being debt-free in FY24 — FCF turned -INR 67 Cr
ROIC of ~18% is moderate for a hospital operator, not exceptional; future capacity additions will dilute returns during ramp-up
red_flags: INR 29 Cr 'Other Income' in FY25 is ~10% of EBIT — likely IPO float interest income, not operational; strips core earnings yield even lower
Reserves jumped from INR 309 Cr (FY23) to INR 1,103 Cr (FY24) via IPO — post-IPO capital base inflates equity, making ROCE optically lower going forward
Free Cash Flow negative in FY21 (-118 Cr) and FY25 (-67 Cr); hospital expansion capex is lumpy and long payback
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: EBIT FY25 = INR 297 Cr. Enterprise Value = Market Cap (INR 8,405 Cr) + Debt (INR 393 Cr) - Cash (INR 368 Cr) = ~INR 8,430 Cr. Earnings Yield = 297/8,430 = 3.52% — an outright fail. My minimum is 12% attractive, 15% very attractive. On ROIC, using stated ROCE of 18% (capital employed ~INR 1,844 Cr), the business passes the 12% floor but falls short of the 25% "excellent" bar. When both metrics are ranked together, this company would land in the bottom quartile of the Magic Formula universe — expensive on earnings yield, mediocre on capital returns.

The business narrative is genuinely improving: revenue CAGR of 22%, operating leverage visible in EBITDA margins expanding from 24% to 25%, and finance costs shrinking sharply as the company paid down debt post-IPO. However, Jupiter is now re-leveraging (INR 403 Cr new borrowings in FY25) to fund a significant expansion (CWIP surged to INR 296 Cr). Hospital bed additions take 3-5 years to generate returns, so near-term ROIC will compress before it improves. The market is pricing in that expansion at a 43.5x P/E — a forward-looking bet I don't make with the Magic Formula, which values only current earning power.
